bib.title: AlpacaFarm: A Simulation Framework for Methods that Learn from Human Feedback

question: Can LLM-simulated human pairwise feedback, an automatic win-rate evaluation and reference implementations let researchers develop methods that learn from human feedback cheaply and have the insights transfer to real human feedback?
hypothesis: Method rankings obtained in simulation (simulated feedback and simulated evaluation) will match rankings obtained with real human feedback and human evaluation.
contributions: LLM prompts simulating human pairwise feedback, cheaper than crowdworkers with high agreement
An automatic evaluation validated against real-world (Alpaca Demo) instructions
Reference implementations of PPO, best-of-n, expert iteration, DPO, Quark, binary FeedME and reward conditioning
End-to-end validation: eleven systems trained/evaluated in simulation vs on 10k real human preference pairs

method.summary: Simulator that replaces crowdworker pairwise labels with a pool of 13 prompted OpenAI-model annotators (plus 25% label flips for training), evaluates by win-rate against Davinci003 on 805 instructions, and implements six learning-from-pairwise-feedback methods on a LLaMA 7B SFT model. Validated by training the same methods on 10k human-labelled pairs and comparing method rankings.
method.task: instruction following; learning from pairwise feedback (RLHF-style) and pairwise LLM-judge evaluation

datasets.name: Alpaca data (AlpacaFarm splits)
datasets.size: 52k (x,y) examples; 42k used: SFT 10k, PREF 10k, unlabeled 20k, validation 2k (10k left unused)

datasets.name: AlpacaFarm evaluation set
datasets.size: 805 instructions: 252 self-instruct, 188 OASST, 129 Anthropic helpful, 80 Vicuna, 156 Koala
datasets.source: public test sets combined to mimic Alpaca Demo

datasets.name: Alpaca Demo instructions
datasets.size: 200 instructions hand-filtered (no PII, toxic, or chatbot-referring)
datasets.source: real user interactions with Alpaca Demo; not released

datasets.name: Human pairwise preferences on PREF split
datasets.size: 10k pairs; approx 20K pairs planned in guideline
datasets.source: Amazon Mechanical Turk, 16 selected of 34 annotators
datasets.preprocessing: 4-way rating binarized; about 18% were 'slightly better' and treated as normal labels

other.note: Davinci003 is the reference model; GPT-4/ChatGPT/Davinci003 also power the simulated annotators

models.name: Surrogate reward model
models.architecture: classifier fine-tuned from SFT base, Bradley-Terry loss

training.objective: SFT; Bradley-Terry reward model (Eq 2); PPO KL-regularised reward (Eq 3); DPO (Eq 1); best-of-n SFT for expert iteration; top-quantile Quark
training.lr: PPO peak 1e-5 decayed to 0; Quark peak 3e-6 decayed to 0; DPO peak 1e-5
training.lr_schedule: PPO and Quark decay to 0; DPO linear warmup then linear decay to 0
training.batch_size: PPO/Quark: 512 rollouts per step, 2 epochs of gradient updates with batch 256; DPO: 64
training.steps: PPO: 10 passes over unlabeled set = 390 steps (peak at 40-80 steps); Quark 390 steps
training.regularisation: PPO KL coefficient 0.02 (human), 0.002 (simulated); Quark KL 0.05; DPO beta 0.1; gradient clip Euclidean norm 1
training.compute: most methods under 2 hrs; best-of-16 sampling for expert iteration about 4 h on 20k unlabeled then under 1 h fine-tune; DPO 1 epoch under 3 h

other.ppo: advantage normalised across whole rollout batch; value model initialised from reward model; GAE lambda=gamma=1; fixed KL coef
other.sft_reward_hparams: SFT and reward-model hyperparameters not stated in text
other.best_of_n: n=1024 in main experiments; optimal n about 16
other.expert_iteration: single round, trained on best-of-16 outputs

inference.temperature: 0.7 for all systems except best-of-n (SFT 10k reranked at 1.0); API models at 0.7
inference.samples: best-of-n: n=1024 (Table 2); no repeat runs or seeds stated
inference.prompting: ChatGPT/GPT-4 system prompt asks for response under 1000 / 500 characters (text says ChatGPT and Davinci003 in one sentence and ChatGPT and GPT-4 in the next)

parameters.annotator_pool: 13 annotators: 5 GPT-4, 4 ChatGPT, 4 Davinci003; sampling temp 1.0, top-p 1.0

metrics.name: win-rate vs Davinci003
metrics.definition: percentage of 805 instructions where the model output is preferred to Davinci003's by simulated (p_eval_sim, no noise) or human annotators

metrics.name: agreement with human majority
metrics.definition: agreement of an annotator with majority vote of 3 human annotations

metrics.name: annotator variance/bias
metrics.definition: variance = error of a held-out annotation vs majority of 3 draws; bias = error between majority of 4 simulated and 4 human annotators

metrics.name: Spearman correlation of method rankings
metrics.definition: simulated vs human win-rates over 11 systems

eval.protocol: Each method M is trained and tuned in simulation, and some are retrained on human preferences with hyperparameter ranges from simulation; both are judged against Davinci003 by simulated and human annotators respectively. Win-rates reported with standard errors. Quark and reward conditioning not run with humans. Single run per method stated.

availability.data: released with the repo (simulator, human preference data); Alpaca Demo data not released

limits: Instructions are simple and single-turn, even the Demo ones
All fine-tuned models start from LLaMA 7B
Human validation from a small crowd (text says 13 crowdworkers; 16 selected, one outlier removed)
Assumes an oracle LLM much stronger than the models studied
Hyperparameters (e.g. KL coefficient) differ between simulated and human feedback
Simulated annotators prefer the first output and outputs from the same model
Rank mismatches: SFT10k vs SFT52k and ChatGPT vs PPO
Judges use 2023 OpenAI models; length bias: ChatGPT shortened prompt makes PPO beat it

lineage.work: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)
Scaling laws for reward model overoptimization (Gao et al.)

figures.caption: The ranking of methods trained and evaluated in AlpacaFarm matches that of methods trained and evaluated in the human-based pipeline.
Simulated annotators are cheap and have a high agreement with human annotators.
The added variability in AlpacaFarm annotators is needed to reproduce reward model over-optimization seen in human data.
figures.why: shows single GPT-4 judge misses over-optimization
